Orthopedics · published research

Flexor tendon injury

One randomized trial reported better passive motion and less pain, while an earlier trial found improvement only in edema and no between-group difference in pain, grip, or function.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One randomized trial reported better passive motion and less pain, while an earlier trial found improvement only in edema and no between-group difference in pain, grip, or function.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Tendons > Digital flexor tendons category contains four unique titles: two randomized human trials and two sheep studies. The human trials concern repaired digital flexor tendons but use different protocols and follow-up. The sheep models are separate preclinical studies and do not add patient cohorts.

Human and clinical evidence

A randomized trial with 97 patients and 114 injured fingers reported that postoperative PBM added to rehabilitation improved passive range of motion and reduced pain compared with its control condition (Poorpezeshk et al. 2018). An earlier randomized trial with 25 patients and 41 injuries found a reduction in edema but no significant between-group difference in pain, grip strength, or functional outcomes (Özkan et al. 2004). These results support a possible effect on motion in one study but do not establish consistent recovery across outcomes.

Animal evidence

Two sheep studies are listed in the exact category. They examine tendon healing in surgical models and provide preclinical evidence only; neither can determine whether patients regain motion, strength, or use of the hand.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo publication was identified in the exact category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The later human trial used combined 660-nm red and 890-nm near-infrared light, with reported fluences of 2 and 5.85 J/cm² over eight to ten sessions in four weeks. The earlier trial used a 904-nm near-infrared laser over ten sessions in two weeks. Differences in wavelength, schedule, surgery, and rehabilitation make direct comparison difficult.

Interpretation

The clinical literature is small and mixed. One trial reports improvements in passive motion and pain, while the other supports only an edema outcome. The animal findings do not resolve the uncertainty about patient function.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for passive range-of-motion improvement after flexor tendon repair Very low for pain, grip strength, and broad functional recovery
Publications and records4 unique titles in the exact category

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two small randomized human trials test PBM after flexor tendon repair and report different outcome patterns. One found better passive range of motion and less pain, while another found a difference only in edema and no added pain or function benefit. The two sheep studies support preclinical interest but cannot resolve these clinical inconsistencies.
